reason: A tangent sliding along the curve lets the student check the derived formula against the actual gradient, including the sign of the $x^{-3/2}$ term.

scenes.title: Checking the derivative against the tangent gradient
scenes.purpose: See that the derivative you found gives the gradient of the curve, so the answer can be checked at any point.

steps.text: The solid curve is $y=\frac{4x^3-3}{2\sqrt{x}}$. Once you split it as $2x^{5/2}-\frac{3}{2}x^{-1/2}$ (the first M1), you can differentiate term by term. Dividing top and bottom separately would not describe this curve's gradient.

The dashed curve is $\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=5x^{3/2}+\frac{3}{4}x^{-3/2}$. The term $5x^{3/2}$ comes from $2\times\frac{5}{2}x^{3/2}$, which earns the first A1 and completes the M1 for lowering the index.
Drag $a$ and watch the tangent at $P$. Its gradient always equals the height of $Q$ on the dashed curve, so the formula is right.

Move $a$ close to $0.3$. The curve is steeply rising here, so the gradient is large and positive. This needs the term $+\frac{3}{4}x^{-3/2}$: two negatives multiply to give a positive, and a wrong sign would give a negative gradient and lose the final A1.

guide.what_you_see: The curve $y=\dfrac{4x^3-3}{2\sqrt{x}}$ from the question (solid), together with the dashed graph of the derivative $5x^{3/2}+\frac{3}{4}x^{-3/2}$ you are asked to find. A tangent to the solid curve at $P$ lets you check that the derivative gives the gradient.

legend.meaning: The curve $y=\dfrac{4x^3-3}{2\sqrt{x}}$ from the question, for $x>0$. It is the same as $2x^{5/2}-\frac{3}{2}x^{-1/2}$ once split into powers of $x$.
The dashed graph of the answer $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=5x^{3/2}+\frac{3}{4}x^{-3/2}$. Its height at $x$ is the claimed gradient of $C$ at $x$.
The point on $C$ with $x$-coordinate $a$, that is $\left(a,\frac{4a^3-3}{2\sqrt{a}}\right)$. It moves when you change the slider $a$.
The point on the dashed graph $D$ directly above or below $P$, at $x=a$. Its height is the value of $5a^{3/2}+\frac{3}{4}a^{-3/2}$.
The tangent to $C$ at $P$. Its gradient is the true gradient of the curve there.
A vertical guide line at $x=a$ joining $P$ and $Q$.

interact.do: Drag $a$ from $0.3$ to $3$, then try the values $1$, $2$ and close to $0.3$.
interact.watch: $P$ and $Q$ move along their curves and the tangent $T$ turns. The height of $Q$ is always the gradient of $T$. At $a=1$ the tangent has gradient $5.75$ and $Q$ has height $5.75$. At $a=2$ both are about $14.4$. Near $a=0.3$ both are about $5.4$, positive even though $C$ is below the axis there, which relies on the $+\frac{3}{4}x^{-3/2}$ term.

question_link.text: The solid curve $C$ is the curve in the question, and splitting it into $2x^{5/2}-\frac{3}{2}x^{-1/2}$ is the first M1 step. The dashed curve $D$ shows the differentiated result, with $5x^{3/2}$ and $+\frac{3}{4}x^{-3/2}$ as the two A1 terms. Matching the height of $Q$ to the tangent gradient at $P$ checks both terms and their signs.

read_off: The live label gives the value of $5x^{3/2}+\frac{3}{4}x^{-3/2}$ at $x=a$, which is the height of $Q$. It should equal the gradient of the tangent $T$ at $P$. For example, it reads $5.75$ when $a=1$.
